stories.title: Predicting nitrogen dioxide column density from the International Wealth Index with a convolutional neural network in Africa
stories.description: In the pursuit of improving socioeconomic living conditions of their populations, many nations struggle to meet their nationally determined contributions (NDCs) under the Paris agreement, and that shortfall makes accountability for emissions reductions critical. The long atmospheric lifetimes of key gases such as carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4) hinder traditional greenhouse gas (GHG) monitoring, because what any one place emits adds only a small excess to a large, well-mixed background. Nitrogen dioxide (NO2) behaves differently: it is short-lived and highly variable in space and time, so satellite instruments resolve its patterns close to source regions. Across the African continent, mapped temporal correlations between NO2 and CO2 are moderate in magnitude but spatially structured and consistently positive. Although we do not use that association to mechanically convert NO2 observations into CO2, we report it as contextual evidence towards NDCs. Given this context, this study asks the following question: to what extent can socioeconomic development at the neighbourhood scale predict NO2 column densities (the amount of NO2 in the air column above that neighbourhood) across Africa? We apply a convolutional neural network (CNN) to gridded International Wealth Index (IWI) estimates and to NO2 observations from the tropospheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), and obtain an average predictive accuracy of $$R^2$$ = 0.56 across the African continent. Because IWI can be projected forward, we also present an illustrative 2030 scenario as a methodological demonstration of the relationship between socioeconomic development and NO2 trajectories. These findings indicate that gridded wealth estimates carry predictive information about NO2 column density in Africa. Such estimates offer a lightweight and scalable screening tool that complements process-based atmospheric monitoring rather than replacing it.

stories.title: RNF130 ameliorates renal injury and inflammation by inhibiting macrophage pyroptosis through ubiquitination degradation of PDCD4 in male mice
stories.description: Macrophage pyroptosis has been identified as a contributor to acute kidney injury (AKI), but the underlying mechanisms involved remain unclear. Herein, we identify that ring finger protein 130 (RNF130) RNF130 is significantly downregulated in both mice and patients with AKI. Myeloid cell-specific loss of RNF130 aggravates renal pathological damage and facilitates macrophage pyroptosis in AKI mouse models. Proteomics analyses and experimental validation show that RNF130 deficiency prevents the ubiquitination of programmed cell death 4 (PDCD4) dependent on the lysine 402 of PDCD4. Activated PDCD4 promotes the phosphorylation of NF-κB and STAT3, triggering NLRP3 inflammasome activation and caspase-1-mediated cleavage of GSDMD, contributing to macrophage pyroptosis. Overexpression of PDCD4 nullifies the beneficial role of RNF130. High-throughput screening of a compound library identified that Nystose effectively mitigated renal injury in ischemic AKI mice by targeting and upregulating RNF130. These findings highlight the potential of RNF130 as a promising target for AKI. Macrophage pyroptosis has been shown to be involved in acute kidney injury (AKI). Here the authors find that ring finger protein 130 (RNF130) is downregulated in AKI and that loss of RNF130 in myeloid cells aggravates renal pathological damage and that RNF130 decreases macrophage pyroptosis through prevention of ubiquitination and inactivation of PDCD4 and that otherwise PDCD4 promotes phosphorylation of NF-kB and STAT3 leading to NLRP3 inflammasome activation and macrophage pyroptosis.

stories.title: Characterizing time-of-day physical activity patterns across cognitive trajectories in older adults: a longitudinal cohort study
stories.description: Declining cognitive function is a growing health challenge, yet how cognitive decline influences time-of-day physical activity (PA) patterns remains underexplored. Among cognitively unimpaired participants from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Study, we modeled general and domain-specific cognitive trajectories and related them to accelerometry-derived PA a median of 8.2 years later in 811 participants (mean baseline age 73.1 years) using function-on-scalar and multivariable regression. Slower cognitive decline was associated with more favorable midday PA (10 AM–3 PM), including higher movement volume, less sedentary time, fewer interruptions to active periods, and greater activity variability. In adjusted linear regression models, associations with PA patterns derived from a window as short as 11 AM-1 PM were comparable to those with 24-hour measures. The executive function trajectory exhibited the strongest associations with PA patterns, and over the longest period of the day; the language trajectory showed non-linear associations, and the peak association for the memory trajectory with PA occurred in the late morning (10:30–11:30 AM). Associations between cognitive decline and activity variability were stronger than for other PA metrics. Our findings highlight the potential of PA patterns, particularly activity variability, as a non-invasive way to help monitor cognitive decline before clinical impairment emerges.
